title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 218: Harnessing the Gale: Wind-Powered Cargo
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 218 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

Harnessing the Gale: The Modern Revival of Wind-Powered Cargo

Paragraph 1. Large cargo ships carry over eighty percent of world trade across oceans. Today, these giant ships burn heavy diesel oil to move forward. However, burning dirty fuel creates about three percent of global warming gases and fills coastal towns with dark smoke. Because international shipping groups want cleaner oceans, ship builders are returning to an old idea with modern technology: using wind to push cargo ships.

Paragraph 2. Modern wind sails look very different from the soft cloth sails on old wooden ships. In 2023, a large cargo ship called the Pyxis Ocean added two tall hard sails called WindWings. Standing nearly thirty-eight metres high, these hard structures look like vertical airplane wings. Smart onboard computers automatically turn the wings to catch the best ocean wind and pull the ship forward. In sea tests, WindWings saved up to three tonnes of fuel every day.

Paragraph 3. Putting giant rigid wings onto cargo ships also brings a practical problem. Cargo ships must pass through narrow canals and sail under tall port cranes and bridges. If tall wings stayed standing straight up, they would crash into these structures. To solve this, engineers built strong folding joints so workers can fold the wings flat on the ship's deck near ports.

Paragraph 4. Captains also use smart computer maps to get the most out of the wind. The software checks live satellite weather maps and ocean waves to pick windy sea paths. Even if a windy path is slightly longer, the free wind power saves far more fuel than going in a straight line.

groups.title: Questions 5–8
groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

steps: Đoạn 1: "...burn heavy diesel oil to move forward."
Đoạn 3: "...sail under tall port cranes and bridges."

q5.text: Why do ship builders want to add wind power to cargo ships?
options: A. Modern engines cannot travel across wide oceans.
B. Sailors miss working on traditional wooden ships.
C. Diesel ships produce harmful gases and smoke.
D. Ocean winds have become faster in recent years.

steps: Đoạn 1: Đốt dầu diesel gây 3% khí nhà kính toàn cầu và khói bụi ở cảng.

q6.text: How are WindWings different from nineteenth-century sails?
options: A. They are rigid structures moved automatically by computers.
B. They are woven from heavy cotton cloth and wood.
C. They require twenty sailors pulling ropes manually.
D. They can only work when ships stay inside harbours.

steps: Đoạn 2: Cánh cứng như cánh máy bay và được máy tính tự động xoay theo hướng gió.

q7.text: What helps WindWings pass safely under port cranes?
options: A. Workers remove the wings completely before arriving.
B. Captains sail only during quiet low-tide hours.
C. Port cranes are rebuilt twice as high as before.
D. Special joints fold the wings down flat on deck.

steps: Đoạn 3: Khớp gập giúp hạ cánh buồm nằm phẳng xuống boong tàu khi vào cảng.

q8.text: What does smart routing software often choose for wind-assisted ships?
options: A. The shortest straight line across calm water
B. A slightly longer sea path that has stronger wind
C. Routes that stay within sight of coastal roads
D. Paths that turn off satellite maps completely

steps: Đoạn 4: Chọn đường đón gió dù dài hơn một chút nhưng tiết kiệm nhiên liệu nhiều hơn.
